video.title: Working in the Wild (Holly Akello)
video.transcript: Narrator: Holly Akello doesn't have an ordinary job! She looks after wild animals at a conservation center in Uganda. Holly is positive and enthusiastic about her job. She likes to be with animals. Holly: I feel so lucky that I'm in the field doing what I've always dreamed of doing. Narrator: The 23-year-old takes care of all kinds of animals-from snakes to hyenas. Some people think it's a dangerous job, but it's always an adventure, and she loves it! At the conservation center, Holly gets training and learns skills she uses every day. She's responsible for preparing food and feeding the lions. She gives them their meal. Then she sits down to spend time and communicate with them. Holly: I'm not afraid of wildlife. Because, I think, if you're able to understand them, it becomes so easy for you to work with them. Narrator: These veterinarians and doctors in Rwanda also think it's important to look after animals. The team of skilled workers help increase the population of mountain gorillas in the wild. The vets carry equipment with them. They study the gorillas and count them. They give names to the new baby gorillas. Gorilla Doctor: See, there is a baby behind, and that baby is on the list to be named. Narrator: They also teach the schoolchildren in the area about the animals. With the help of the team, the future for these gorillas looks positive! Gorilla Doctor: It's all about teamwork. And of course, each piece makes a difference. Narrator: You need special skills to work with wild animals every day. And you need to be curious and love adventure-just like these people.

video.title: A Shared Memory
video.transcript: Narrator: When we share a memory together, it can bring us a lot of happiness. These women met almost 50 years ago. Today, they're seeing each other for the first time in many years. Woman: We're getting together a bunch of women from the first Women's Outward Bound back in 1965. Narrator: They all met when they were teenagers on an outdoor adventure program. In 1965, Outward Bound was a new course for girls. At that time, young women in the U.S. didn't get to do a lot of difficult outdoor activities. Woman: It all began for me when I was sixteen years old, after I heard a woman talking on the radio. I heard this woman talking about something called Outward Bound. So when I got home, I told my mother about this program. I wanted to go to the first one just for girls. Narrator: To complete the course, the women spent a month in the wilderness. And for three days, they each stayed in the woods alone-with no tent and no food. Today, the women return to the school. The group has the chance to relive their experiences. For the first time since 1965, they stay in one of the cabins. When they were teenagers, they often got up early and swam in the cold lake. So today, they swim again. They loved canoeing together, so they try that again. It brings back lots of emotions. They sit around the campfire and share memories. They found courage. And they made great friends for life.

audio.title: Exploring Work (Full Script)
audio.transcript: Narrator: Different people have different views about 'big cats,' such as lions and jaguars. Some think the animals are beautiful, but others are afraid of them because they can be dangerous. Thandiwe Mweetwa and Ricardo Samuel Moreno are biologists. Thandiwe helps lions in Zambia. Sometimes people kill these animals because they want to protect their farm animals. Host: Today we talk with Annie Griffiths. She's a photographer for the National Geographic Society. Annie: Sometimes my work takes me to dangerous places like mountains or jungles. Host: Why do you explore the world? Annie: It allows me to learn about different cultures and different views. I spend time with ordinary people. Host: How do you communicate? Annie: I'll gesture or smile so that people feel more relaxed around me. Host: Do you need special skills? Annie: I think the most important thing is curiosity. Candidate: The job advertisement says you provide training. Interviewer: We can train you to use the equipment. We want to hire positive people. Narrator: Explorers can also be journalists, scientists, and filmmakers. Bertie Gregory manages film projects. He's responsible for Epic Adventures. Step two is to learn about photography. Practice taking pictures. You don't need expensive equipment. If you know a few words of the language, it can help you meet people.

audio.title: Good Times (Full Script)
audio.transcript: Narrator: Nostalgia can be both a good and a bad emotion. Describe a feeling of sadness when you think about the past. Japan: natsukashii is more positive. An object like a train ticket can remind you of a holiday. Speaker: When I got up this morning, I smelled fresh coffee. It reminds me of my childhood and my father. Nostalgia starts with a memory. A doctor created the word in 1688 to describe soldiers who missed their homes. Some thought nostalgia was dangerous. Today, it is positive and useful. It helps with changes. Thinking about old schools can relax you. Doctors play music for older people. Brain becomes more active. Researchers discovered humans can remember about 5,000 faces. Faces are more memorable than names. Wilma Bainbridge is a neuroscientist and researcher. From her work, she knows color and appearance are important for memory. We remember 60 percent of photos because of color. We remember photos with people in them. Scientists still do not know the answer to some memory questions. Three ways to make more memories: Use the Ten-Year Test. Try 'Firsts' - stay in memories forever. Don't always go the easiest way. Take a different road.
